sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
On a full-moon night in winter, the Great Rann of Kutch is a floor of salt so white that people walk out onto it at midnight and read by the light. Six months earlier the same ground was under water. A few hundred kilometres south, in the dry teak forest of Gir, live the only wild lions left in Asia: 891 of them in the May 2025 count, up from perhaps a couple of dozen a century ago.

Between those two places sits a state that gave India Gandhi, Patel and the Amul girl, cuts most of the world's diamonds, breaks old ships on a beach, refines more crude oil at one site than anywhere on earth, and has banned alcohol since the day it was born, 1 May 1960.

Gujarat is a trading coast first. Its people sailed to Africa and Southeast Asia two thousand years before they ran motels in America. Today you meet it through things you can see: a stepwell that goes down seven floors, a sari woven twice, a lion with a belly fold, a kite string coated in glass.

sections.title: Gujarat at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat is India's westernmost big state, a wedge of land between the Arabian Sea and Rajasthan, with Pakistan's Sindh across the salt marsh to the north-west. It was carved out of the old bilingual Bombay State on **1 May 1960**, the same day Maharashtra was born.

It is the **fifth-largest** state by area, **196,024 km²**, and had **6.04 crore** people in the 2011 census, ninth in India. In April 2025 the Ministry of Ports adopted a new way of measuring coasts that counts bays and creeks; Gujarat's coastline went from about 1,600 km to **2,340.62 km**, the longest of any state. Vav-Tharad, carved from Banaskantha on 2 October 2025, made it **34 districts**.

The capital is **Gandhinagar**, a planned city built in the 1960s next to **Ahmedabad**, the biggest city. The economy is about 8% of India's on the state's own count, heavy in factories, ports and chemicals. The language is Gujarati. The six numbers below are the ones to remember.

sections.title: The land: salt, lions and a long coast
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat has three parts you can see on a map. **Kutch** in the north-west is a block of rocky upland ringed by the salt marshes of the Great and Little Rann. **Saurashtra** (also called Kathiawar) is the round peninsula in the middle, low hills and dry farmland with Gir forest and Girnar near its south. The **mainland** to the east is flat, fertile and crossed by rivers: the Sabarmati past Ahmedabad, the Mahi, the Narmada and the Tapi at Surat.

Two gulfs cut in from the sea. The Gulf of Kutch holds India's first marine national park, declared in 1982, with corals and sea slugs exposed at low tide. The Gulf of Khambhat has some of the highest tides in India, which matters later for the ship-breakers of Alang.

Rain is low and unreliable in Kutch and north Gujarat and heavy in the south. Water, not land, has always been the limit, which is why stepwells, reservoirs at Dholavira and the Narmada canal keep turning up in this story.

spotlights.name: The White Rann

where.label: Great Rann of Kutch, near Dhordo

spotlights.spot_it: A flat white salt crust to the horizon, cracked into polygons; pink at sunset, silver under a full moon.
spotlights.story_md: The Great Rann of Kutch is a seasonal salt marsh of roughly 7,500 km², one of the largest in the world. It is not a sand desert. In the monsoon the sea and rivers push in and flood it a few feet deep; Kutch becomes nearly an island. From October the water evaporates and leaves a crust of salt that hardens enough to walk on. The border with Pakistan runs through it. At Dhordo, the village at its edge that runs the winter festival, the white floor starts where the road ends.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains Kutch: half the year an island, half the year joined to the mainland by a white plain.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under water in August, white as paper in December.

spotlights.name: The Asiatic lion of Gir

where.label: Gir National Park, Junagadh and Gir Somnath

spotlights.spot_it: Smaller mane than an African lion, so the ears show; a long fold of skin runs along the belly.
spotlights.story_md: Asiatic lions once ranged from Greece to Bengal. By the early 1900s hunting had pushed the last of them into the Gir forest of the Nawab of Junagadh, who banned shooting them. Gir became a sanctuary in 1965. The 16th census in May 2025 counted **891** lions, up from 674 in 2020, and for the first time more than half were living outside the protected forest, in farmland, coastal scrub and around Porbandar, Dwarka and Rajkot. Herders here have lived next to lions for generations; attacks on people are rare, but cattle kills are common.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every wild Asiatic lion on earth lives in one Indian state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Look for the belly fold: Asia's lion wears a crease.

compare.difference: The Asiatic male's mane is shorter and sparser, and a belly fold runs the length of the body.

spotlights.name: Indian wild ass (khur)
spotlights.spot_it: A sandy-brown donkey-like animal with a dark stripe down the back and a white belly, running fast across bare mud flats.
spotlights.story_md: The khur is the last population of its subspecies, and it lives only in Gujarat, mostly in the Little Rann of Kutch, a 4,950 km² sanctuary declared in 1972. In 1976 there were about 720. The 2024 count, using drones and camera traps, found **7,672**, up from 6,082 in 2020. They can run at about 70 km/h. They share the flats with salt workers, who pan salt in the same months the asses graze the scrub islands called bets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare conservation recovery: tenfold in fifty years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven thousand wild asses and not a tree in sight.

spotlights.name: Girnar
spotlights.spot_it: A cluster of granite peaks near Junagadh with white Jain temples on its flanks and a stone stair of nearly ten thousand steps.
spotlights.story_md: Girnar is a volcanic massif whose highest peak, Gorakhnath, is about 1,069 m, the highest point in Gujarat. Pilgrims of several faiths climb it. Jains revere it as the place where Neminath, the 22nd Tirthankara, gained liberation; the marble temples two-thirds up date from the 12th century. Hindu sadhus gather at the Dattatreya peak, and the Bhavnath fair at the foot each Shivaratri draws naga ascetics. Since October 2020 a 2.3 km ropeway does in eight minutes what the steps do in a morning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One hill, three faiths, and the state's highest ground.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten thousand steps or eight minutes in a cable car.

spotlights.name: Sardar Sarovar Dam
spotlights.spot_it: A long concrete wall across the Narmada, 163 m high, with the Statue of Unity standing just downstream.
spotlights.story_md: Nehru laid the foundation stone in 1961. The dam was finished only in 2017, after decades of court fights led by the Narmada Bachao Andolan, which argued that the reservoir would drown villages of Adivasi and farming families in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat without fair resettlement. Its canals now carry Narmada water hundreds of kilometres to dry Saurashtra and Kutch, and its dam height makes it one of the largest concrete gravity dams in the world. Both stories are true at once: water for millions, and a long fight over who paid for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why taps run in towns that used to rely on tankers, and a lasting case study in who bears the cost of big projects.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-six years from foundation stone to full height.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
The 2011 census counted **60,439,692** people, 5% of India. A new census is under way and will replace these figures. Density was **308** per km², a little below India's 382, because Kutch is nearly empty while the Ahmedabad to Surat belt is crowded.

Gujarat is more urban than most of India: **42.6%** lived in towns in 2011, against 31% nationally. Literacy was **78.03%**, above the national 73%. The weak number is the sex ratio, **919** women per 1,000 men, below India's 943, and lower still among young children, a sign of sex-selective abortion that the state has been slow to shake off.

Hindus were 88.6% of people, Muslims 9.7%, Jains about 1% and Christians 0.5%. The Jain share is small, but Jain merchants, temples and food rules shape the state far beyond their numbers.

sections.title: Deep history: Harappans to Solankis
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat has more excavated Harappan sites than any other Indian state. Dholavira and Lothal are the famous two, but Rangpur, Surkotada and dozens more show that the Indus civilisation lived along this coast and in Kutch from about 3000 BCE.

In historic times the region was a prize. The Mauryas held it, then the Western Kshatrapas, then the Guptas, whose inscriptions all sit on one rock at Junagadh. The Maitrakas ruled from Vallabhi, a Buddhist university town, from about 475 to 776 CE. Then came the **Chaulukyas**, also called Solankis, who ruled from Anhilwad Patan from 942 to about 1244. Their age gave Gujarat the Modhera Sun Temple, Rani ki Vav, the Rudra Mahalaya at Siddhpur and the marble Jain temples at Mount Abu and Girnar.

In 1026 Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Somnath. The Solankis rebuilt and kept ruling for two more centuries. In 1299 Alauddin Khalji's army took the region and the Hindu kingdoms of the plains ended.

spotlights.name: Dholavira
spotlights.spot_it: Stone walls and giant cut reservoirs on a salt-marsh island in Kutch; a city laid out in three nested parts.
spotlights.story_md: Dholavira sits on Khadir Bet, an island in the Great Rann. It was a Harappan city for about 1,500 years, from roughly 3000 BCE. Its builders lived with almost no rain, so they cut a chain of stone reservoirs and dammed two seasonal streams to fill them. Near the north gate lay ten Indus script signs, each about 37 cm tall, made of white gypsum inlay: possibly the oldest signboard in the world, still unread. Found in 1967-68, dug from 1990 by R. S. Bisht, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the Harappans at their most ingenious: a city designed around water.
spotlights.memory_hook: A signboard 4,500 years old that nobody can read.

spotlights.name: Lothal
spotlights.spot_it: A long rectangular brick basin beside low brick walls, near the head of the Gulf of Khambhat.
spotlights.story_md: Lothal was a Harappan town of bead-makers and traders. Between 1955 and 1960 the archaeologist S. R. Rao dug out a brick basin about 220 m long and argued that it was a dock connected to an old course of the Sabarmati, the earliest known in the world. Seals from the Persian Gulf found here support the idea of sea trade. Some scholars think the basin was a water tank for irrigation instead. The dock reading is popular and may be right, but it is not settled. A National Maritime Heritage Complex is being built next to the site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It puts Gujarat's seafaring back more than four thousand years.
spotlights.memory_hook: World's first dock, or a very large water tank: the bricks are not telling.

spotlights.name: The Junagadh rock
spotlights.spot_it: A single granite boulder under a shed at the foot of Girnar, its face crowded with three sets of ancient writing.
spotlights.story_md: On one rock, three empires left a message. Around 250 BCE Ashoka had fourteen of his edicts carved here. About 150 CE the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman added a long inscription in Sanskrit, one of the earliest long Sanskrit texts in stone, recording that he had repaired the Sudarshana lake, a reservoir first built under Chandragupta Maurya, after a storm burst its dam. Around 456 CE the Gupta emperor Skandagupta recorded yet another repair of the same lake. Seven centuries of water engineering, on one boulder.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest public record of a dam repair in India, and proof that Gujarat mattered to every big empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: One rock, three emperors, one leaky lake.

spotlights.name: Modhera Sun Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A sandstone temple behind a deep stepped tank lined with 108 small shrines; carved dancers cover every pillar.
spotlights.story_md: Bhima I of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty built the temple to Surya in 1026-27, the same years Mahmud of Ghazni raided Somnath. In front is the Surya Kund, a rectangular tank of steps and tiny shrines that looks like an inverted pyramid. The sanctum was planned so that sunlight fell on the deity at the equinoxes. Worship here ended long ago; the image is gone. In October 2022 Modhera village was declared India's first round-the-clock solar-powered village, a neat rhyme for a temple to the sun.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the high point of the Solanki style that also built Rani ki Vav.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple to the sun, a village that runs on it.

spotlights.name: Rani ki Vav
spotlights.spot_it: A stepwell that descends seven levels, its walls packed with about 500 carved gods, goddesses and apsaras.
spotlights.story_md: Around 1063 the widowed queen Udayamati built this stepwell at Patan in memory of King Bhima I. It is designed as an upside-down temple, so you walk down through the shrine toward water. It is about 64 m long and 27 m deep, with more than 500 principal sculptures, many of Vishnu's avatars. Floods of the Saraswati later buried it in silt, which is why the carving is so sharp; the Archaeological Survey dug it out in the 1980s. UNESCO listed it in 2014, and since 2018 it has been on the back of the lavender ₹100 note.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the finest stepwell in India, and the silt that buried it is why it survived.
spotlights.memory_hook: Check your ₹100 note: the queen's well is on the back.

sections.title: Sultans, Mughals and the richest port in India
sections.intro_md:
From 1407 to 1573 Gujarat was an independent **sultanate**, rich from the cotton and indigo trade and the pilgrim route to Mecca. Its rulers built Ahmedabad, Champaner and a style of mosque that borrowed freely from Hindu and Jain temples, because the same Gujarati masons built both. Sultan Bahadur Shah died in 1537 off Diu, fighting the Portuguese, who then held Diu and Daman until 1961.

Akbar conquered Gujarat in 1572-73. Under the Mughals, **Surat** became the empire's main port. The English beat a Portuguese fleet at Swally near Surat in 1612 and opened their first trading post in India there in 1613. The East India Company's Indian story starts in Gujarat, not Bengal.

In the 18th century the Marathas took most of the plains; the Gaekwads ruled Baroda. The British took the rest step by step, but left more than 200 princely states in Saurashtra and Kutch, from Junagadh to tiny estates of a few villages. That patchwork lasted until 1948.

spotlights.name: Old Ahmedabad and its pols
spotlights.spot_it: Gated lanes of carved wooden houses, a bird-feeding tower (chabutro) in the square, a single gate shut at night.
spotlights.story_md: Sultan Ahmed Shah founded Ahmedabad on the Sabarmati in 1411 and began the Bhadra fort. Its old city grew as **pols**: dead-end neighbourhoods behind one gate, each often home to one caste or trade, with a secret back passage in many for escape during riots. Houses have carved wooden facades, inner courtyards and underground tanks for rainwater. Most squares have a chabutro, a tall feeding post for birds, because Jain and Vaishnav households feed birds daily. In 2017 the walled city became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The pols are a working model of how a merchant city protected itself.
spotlights.memory_hook: One gate, one community, one tower for the birds.

spotlights.name: Sidi Saiyyed jali
spotlights.spot_it: A stone window in which a tree's branches twist into a lace screen; usually photographed from inside with light behind it.
spotlights.story_md: Sidi Saiyyed, an Abyssinian noble in the Gujarat Sultan's army, built this small mosque in 1572-73, the last year before Akbar took Gujarat. Its west windows are filled with stone screens, or jalis, carved from single slabs, and the most famous shows a tree of life with intertwined branches and a palm. It has become Ahmedabad's unofficial emblem: the logo of IIM Ahmedabad is based on it. The mosque has no minarets; work stopped when the Mughals arrived.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the city's most copied image, made by an African-born patron.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tree carved so thin you can see the sun through the stone.

spotlights.name: Adalaj stepwell
spotlights.spot_it: Five storeys of carved stone galleries stepping down to an octagonal well; cool even in May.
spotlights.story_md: Rana Veer Singh of the Vaghela dynasty began this stepwell in 1498 and died in battle against Mahmud Begada. Tradition says his widow Rudabai agreed to marry the sultan only if he finished the well, and then threw herself into it. The story cannot be checked. The building can: it mixes Hindu and Jain carving with Islamic floral patterns, and the temperature at the bottom is several degrees lower than at the top, which is why villagers came here to draw water and to rest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Stepwells were public buildings, often paid for by women, built for water and shade.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sultan's deal sealed with a well, if you believe the guides.

spotlights.name: Champaner-Pavagadh
spotlights.spot_it: A ruined sultanate city at the foot of a steep hill, its Jami Masjid with two slim minarets and a carved central arch.
spotlights.story_md: Mahmud Begada captured the Rajput hill fort of Pavagadh in 1484 and built a new capital, Champaner, below it. The Jami Masjid, finished in 1513, mixes temple carving with mosque plans and influenced later Mughal mosques. When the Mughal Humayun took the city in 1535, the capital moved back to Ahmedabad and Champaner emptied, which is why so much survives. It became a UNESCO site in 2004. On the hilltop, the Kalika Mata temple got a new spire and flag in June 2022, the first in about five centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A whole sultanate capital preserved by being abandoned.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital that lived 50 years and has been quiet for 500.

sections.title: From Gandhi to a state of its own
sections.intro_md:
Two Gujaratis shaped the end of the Raj. **Gandhi**, born in Porbandar in 1869, ran his movement from an Ahmedabad ashram. **Vallabhbhai Patel**, a lawyer from Nadiad, earned the title Sardar leading the Bardoli peasants' tax revolt in 1928 and later folded more than 560 princely states into India. Junagadh's Nawab chose Pakistan in 1947; India held a plebiscite there in February 1948 and the vote went overwhelmingly to India.

After independence Saurashtra and Kutch were separate units for a few years, then merged into Bombay State in 1956. Four years of agitation produced Gujarat in 1960.

The state's recent history has hard chapters. The 2001 earthquake killed about 20,000. On 27 February 2002, 59 people, mostly Hindu pilgrims, died when a train coach burned at Godhra; the riots that followed killed 1,044 people by official count, about three quarters of them Muslim, and other estimates run near 2,000. Courts, commissions and journalists have argued over responsibility ever since. Narendra Modi was Chief Minister from 2001 to 2014 and then became Prime Minister, which made Gujarat's development record a national argument.

spotlights.name: Sabarmati Ashram
spotlights.spot_it: Low white cottages with tiled roofs on the riverbank in Ahmedabad; a charkha on the floor of the main room.
spotlights.story_md: Gandhi came back from South Africa in 1915 and set up his first Indian ashram in Ahmedabad, moving it to the bank of the Sabarmati in 1917. For thirteen years this was his base. Ahmedabad's textile mill owners, notably Ambalal Sarabhai, funded him even as he led their workers in a strike in 1918. He walked out of the ashram on 12 March 1930 and vowed not to return until India was free. He never lived here again. A government plan to rebuild the surrounding area, announced in 2024, has been criticised by some Gandhians.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The headquarters of the freedom movement was a cluster of village huts.
spotlights.memory_hook: He left on a walk in 1930 and never came home.

spotlights.name: The Salt March
spotlights.spot_it: Gandhi with a staff at the head of a column of men in white, walking dirt roads to the sea.
spotlights.story_md: Britain taxed salt and banned Indians from making it. On 12 March 1930 Gandhi left Sabarmati with 78 followers and walked about 385 km in 24 days through Gujarati villages to Dandi on the coast. On the morning of 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt from the mud. The act was small and legal nonsense to the British, and that was the point: millions copied it. About 60,000 Indians were jailed within weeks. Newsreels carried the march around the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a tax into a symbol anyone could break.
spotlights.memory_hook: 24 days, 385 km, one handful of salt.

spotlights.name: The Mahagujarat movement
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial pillar with a raised torch near Lal Darwaja, Ahmedabad, listing the names of students killed in 1956.
spotlights.story_md: In 1956 the new states were drawn by language, but Gujarati and Marathi speakers were kept together in a large bilingual Bombay State. On 8 August 1956 students marched in Ahmedabad for a separate Gujarati state; police fired and several were killed. The movement that followed, led by the veteran Indulal Yagnik, ran for four years alongside the Samyukta Maharashtra movement on the other side. On 1 May 1960 Bombay State was split. Ahmedabad was the first capital; Gandhinagar took over in 1970.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gujarat was not handed out; it was won on the street.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born 1 May 1960, twin of Maharashtra.

spotlights.name: The 2001 Kutch earthquake and Smritivan
spotlights.spot_it: A terraced memorial garden on Bhujiyo hill above Bhuj, with the names of about 13,000 victims on plaques.
spotlights.story_md: At 8:46 am on 26 January 2001, Republic Day, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Kutch. Around 20,000 people died, Bhuj and Anjar were flattened and about 400,000 homes collapsed. Kutch rebuilt fast with tax breaks that brought ports and factories, and today it is one of the state's fastest-growing districts. Smritivan, a memorial park and museum on the hill above Bhuj, opened in 2022; in December 2024 it won a special Prix Versailles prize for museum interiors at UNESCO in Paris.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The disaster that remade Kutch's economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Republic Day 2001, 8:46 am: the morning Kutch fell.

sections.title: Language: Gujarati
sections.intro_md:
Gujarati is an Indo-Aryan language that split from Old Western Rajasthani around the 14th century. The poet-saint Narsinh Mehta of Junagadh, in the 15th century, wrote the bhajan 'Vaishnav jan to' that Gandhi made famous. Gujarati has dialects you can hear: Kathiawadi in Saurashtra, Surti in Surat, and in the far west Kutchi, which is closer to Sindhi and usually written in Gujarati script.

Here is a strange fact about modern South Asia. Gandhi, the father of India, wrote his autobiography in Gujarati. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, grew up in a Gujarati-speaking Khoja family whose roots were in Paneli in Kathiawar. Two founders of two nations, both from Gujarati homes.

Useful words: **kem cho** (how are you), **majama** (fine), **aavjo** (goodbye, literally 'come again'), **ben** (sister, added to women's names) and **bhai** (brother).

spotlights.name: Gujarati script
spotlights.spot_it: Letters that look like Devanagari with the top line removed: rounded shapes floating free, no bar joining them.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarati is written in its own script, descended from the same Brahmi family as Devanagari. The quick test: Hindi letters hang from a horizontal line called the shirorekha; Gujarati letters do not. Merchants used a fast, line-less hand for accounts for centuries, and that is where the look comes from. The word for a Gujarati shop ledger, chopda, is still worshipped at Diwali when new account books open. Gujarati had about **5.55 crore** native speakers in 2011, and it is one of the most spoken Indian languages in the US, UK and Canada.
spotlights.why_it_matters: You can tell a Gujarati signboard from a Hindi one in half a second.
spotlights.memory_hook: No roof on the letters: that is Gujarati.

compare.difference: Devanagari joins letters under a continuous top line; Gujarati drops it.

spotlights.name: Narmad
spotlights.spot_it: Turbaned poet in old photographs; his line 'Jai Jai Garavi Gujarat' is the state's anthem.
spotlights.story_md: Narmadashankar Dave (1833 to 1886), known as Narmad, was a Surat poet who wrote that he would live by his pen alone, unusual in his time. He argued for widow remarriage and against caste rules, compiled the first Gujarati dictionary, Narmakosh, and in 1873 wrote 'Jai Jai Garavi Gujarat', still sung as the state song. He is often called the father of modern Gujarati prose. Gujarat's literary award for young writers and Surat's central library carry his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave Gujarati its first dictionary and its anthem.
spotlights.memory_hook: Narmad wrote the dictionary, then the song.

sections.title: Faith: Shiva's sea temple, Krishna's city, a Jain hill
sections.intro_md:
Most Gujaratis are Hindu, and their faith leans to **Krishna** and the goddess. Vaishnav sects such as the Pushtimarg of Vallabhacharya and the Swaminarayan movement, founded in the early 1800s, are strong among merchant families; the Swaminarayan BAPS order built Akshardham in Gandhinagar in 1992 and temples across the diaspora.

**Jains** are about 1% of people but have shaped the state's food, banking and charity. Palitana, Girnar and Taranga are among their holiest hills. **Muslims**, about 10%, include Bohra, Khoja and Memon trading communities with long links to East Africa and the Gulf, and Sufi shrines such as Sarkhej Roza. **Parsis** landed here more than a thousand years ago and kept their fire.

Pilgrimage is the main tourism: Somnath, Dwarka, Ambaji, Palitana and Pavagadh together draw tens of millions of visits a year.

spotlights.name: Somnath
spotlights.spot_it: A tall honey-coloured temple on the sea at Prabhas Patan; an arrow pillar on the seawall points to the South Pole.
spotlights.story_md: Somnath is the first of the twelve jyotirlingas of Shiva. Mahmud of Ghazni looted it in January 1026, and the temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times over the next seven centuries; by the 1800s it was a ruin. Patel pushed for a rebuild after 1947, and President Rajendra Prasad opened the new temple on 11 May 1951, over Nehru's objection to the head of state attending. On the seawall, the Baan Stambh pillar notes that there is no land in a straight line from here to the South Pole. In January 2026 a four-day Somnath Swabhiman Parv marked 1,000 years since the raid.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most charged symbol of destruction and rebuilding in Indian memory.
spotlights.memory_hook: Next stop south: Antarctica.

spotlights.name: Dwarkadhish temple
spotlights.spot_it: A five-storey spire on the westernmost tip of Saurashtra, with a huge triangular flag flying from the top.
spotlights.story_md: Dwarka is Krishna's city in the Mahabharata and one of the four dhams, the cardinal pilgrimages. The present temple, with its 72 pillars and 78 m spire, is mostly from the 15th and 16th centuries. Divers and archaeologists, led by S. R. Rao in the 1980s, found stone structures and anchors under the sea offshore; whether they are the legendary city is disputed. In February 2024 the 2.3 km Sudarshan Setu opened to Bet Dwarka island, India's longest cable-stayed bridge.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anchors Gujarat's Krishna devotion, the root of garba's raas and Vaishnav merchant culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna's city: one on land, one maybe under the sea.

spotlights.name: Palitana (Shatrunjaya)
spotlights.spot_it: A hilltop crowded with hundreds of white marble spires, reached by more than 3,500 stone steps; pilgrims carried up in cloth chairs.
spotlights.story_md: Shatrunjaya hill above Palitana holds about 863 Jain temples built over 900 years, the largest temple cluster in the world on one hill. It is a city of gods only: everyone, priests included, must come down by evening, because no one may spend the night. Pilgrims climb barefoot before dawn. In 2014, after Jain monks went on hunger strike, the state banned the sale of meat and eggs in Palitana town, which was widely called the world's first vegetarian city. The ban was challenged in the High Court and the label is still argued over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the reach of Jain wealth and piety in Gujarat.
spotlights.memory_hook: 863 temples, no overnight guests.

spotlights.name: Udvada Atash Behram
spotlights.spot_it: A plain columned building in a small coastal town; only Parsis may enter to see the fire.
spotlights.story_md: Zoroastrians fleeing Persia landed on the Gujarat coast at Sanjan, by their own tradition around the 8th century. The sacred fire they consecrated, the Iranshah, has burned ever since and has been kept at Udvada since 1742. It is the oldest continuously burning fire of its rank in the Parsi world. The famous story that the Parsi leader convinced the local king by stirring sugar into a full glass of milk does not appear in the 1599 text Qissa-i Sanjan; it is a later legend. Parsis still speak Gujarati at home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Parsis who built Bombay's industry began as Gujarati refugees.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fire lit by refugees, burning for over a thousand years.

spotlights.name: Ambaji
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble temple with a golden spire in the Aravalli hills of Banaskantha; inside, no idol, only a veiled sacred yantra.
spotlights.story_md: Ambaji is one of the Shakti Peethas, tied by tradition to the heart of the goddess Sati. Its most unusual feature: there is no image of the goddess. Priests worship a geometric yantra, and devotees are not supposed to look at it directly; it is draped so that it appears to be a figure. The temple draws huge crowds at the Bhadarvi Poonam fair each autumn, when lakhs of pilgrims walk there from across north Gujarat, and the garba that Gujarat dances in Navratri is, at root, a dance to this goddess.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the devotional centre of Gujarat's goddess worship and of garba.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple where the goddess is a diagram.

sections.title: Dance, music and theatre
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat's performing arts are mostly **communal**, not courtly. There is no Gujarati classical dance on India's official list of eight; instead there are circle dances that anyone can join, devotional singing, and travelling folk theatre.

Navratri is when it all comes out. Garba and dandiya raas fill school grounds, housing society courtyards and giant ticketed venues for nine nights. The music has moved from women's songs with clapping, through dhol and shehnai, to live bands with electric keyboards; songs by singers such as Falguni Pathak sell out stadiums in Mumbai as well as Gujarat.

Other strands are older and quieter: **bhajans** from Narsinh Mehta and Mirabai, the **dayro** (an evening of stories and songs in Saurashtra), the bhavai stage, and the African-rooted dhamal of the Siddis.

rows.garba: One big circle round a lamp

spotlights.name: Garba

where.label: Statewide; biggest grounds in Vadodara and Ahmedabad

spotlights.spot_it: A huge circle of dancers moving anticlockwise around a lamp or shrine, clapping and turning on a three-step beat.
spotlights.story_md: Garba takes its name from garbha, womb: the original centre of the dance is a clay pot with holes, the garbo, with a lamp inside. Women circled it on the nine nights of Navratri singing to the goddess Amba. Today garba grounds in Ahmedabad and Vadodara hold tens of thousands of dancers at once, with live bands and a 'Navratri vacation' in some schools. Steps have names: be taali (two claps), tran taali (three claps), and the fast hinch. UNESCO listed Garba of Gujarat as Intangible Cultural Heritage in December 2023, India's 15th entry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single biggest shared ritual in the state, done on the same nine nights by millions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Garba circles a womb with a flame in it.

compare.difference: Garba is danced with hands and claps; dandiya raas with a pair of sticks struck with a partner.

spotlights.name: Dandiya raas
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers face each other in two lines and strike decorated sticks, then move on to the next partner.
spotlights.story_md: Dandiya raas comes from the raas of Krishna and the gopis, and the sticks are said to stand for swords in the goddess Durga's fight with the demon Mahishasura. Lines move in opposite directions so each dancer meets a new partner every few beats. In the past men and women danced it separately; now it is the late-night second half of most Navratri events, after garba. Saurashtra has its own men's stick dances, such as the Mer community's swirling maniyaro raas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is what most of the world thinks of as 'Gujarati dance'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Click, turn, new partner, click.

spotlights.name: Siddi dhamal
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in peacock-feather skirts with painted faces, drumming on the large mugarman drum and coconut-shell rattles.
spotlights.story_md: The Siddis are Indians of East African descent, brought to Gujarat over centuries as sailors, soldiers and slaves; some rose to power, like the patron of the Sidi Saiyyed mosque. Today a few thousand live in Gujarat, many around Jambur and Sirvan near Gir. Their dhamal dance, performed at Sufi shrines of their saint Bava Gor, keeps rhythms and words with African roots, with a wild finale where dancers toss coconuts into the air and break them on their heads.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is living proof of Gujarat's ancient sea ties to Africa.
spotlights.memory_hook: Africa's drum in a Gujarati forest.

sections.title: Crafts and textiles
sections.intro_md:
Kutch alone has more living textile traditions than many countries. Herders, farmers and merchant castes each developed their own embroidery, and their women could read a stranger's community, village and marital status from the stitches on her clothes.

After the 2001 earthquake, craft became one of Kutch's routes back. NGOs, design schools and buyers arrived, and villages like Bhujodi (weaving), Nirona (rogan, lacquer, bells), Ajrakhpur (block print) and Hodka (embroidery) became places that visitors seek out. Ahmedabad's National Institute of Design, founded in 1961, trained many of the designers who work with them.

Other traditions to know but not covered below: Mata ni pachedi, a painted cloth shrine of the Vaghri community in Ahmedabad; Sankheda lacquered furniture; and Surat's zari metal thread.

spotlights.name: Patan patola
spotlights.spot_it: A silk sari with sharp-edged geometric patterns that look identical on both sides; elephants, parrots and flower lattices.
spotlights.story_md: Patola is double ikat: both the warp and weft threads are tied and dyed in sections before weaving, so the pattern appears as the threads cross on the loom. A thread out of place spoils the design. In Patan only a few Salvi families still weave it, and one sari can take six months to a year. Tradition says King Kumarapala brought Salvi weavers to Patan in the 12th century. Patola were traded to Indonesia, where they became royal cloth. A Gujarati saying holds that a patola may tear, but its colour never fades.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the hardest textiles in the world to make, and a few families keep it alive.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dyed twice before it is woven once.

spotlights.name: Bandhani
spotlights.spot_it: Cloth covered with thousands of tiny dots, each a small raised ring, often red, yellow or black.
spotlights.story_md: Bandhani is tie-dye at the scale of a fingernail. Women pinch the cloth and tie each dot with thread, sometimes using a long fingernail or a metal ring to lift the fabric; a fine piece can have tens of thousands of knots. The cloth is dyed, the knots are pulled, and the dots appear. Kutch and Jamnagar are the centres, and Jamnagar's water is believed locally to give a brighter red. Gujarati brides wear the panetar, white with a red border, and the gharchola, a red grid of bandhani and gold thread.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dots tell you where it came from and what occasion it is for.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every dot is a knot someone tied by hand.

spotlights.name: Rogan painting
spotlights.spot_it: Raised, glossy lines of colour on dark cloth, folded while wet so one side prints onto the other in mirror symmetry.
spotlights.story_md: Rogan begins with castor oil boiled for about twelve hours until it turns into a thick paste, then mixed with pigment. The artist rolls a thread of paste on the palm and lays it on cloth with a metal stylus that never touches the fabric. Half a design is painted and the cloth is folded to print the other half. In the village of Nirona in Kutch, the Khatri family has kept it going for generations. In 2014 Narendra Modi gave Barack Obama a rogan tree of life. Abdul Gafur Khatri received the Padma Shri in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A near-dead craft revived by one family.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paint made of castor oil, drawn in the air.

spotlights.name: Ajrakh
spotlights.spot_it: Block-printed cloth in deep indigo and madder red with dense star and lattice patterns, printed on both sides.
spotlights.story_md: Ajrakh is a resist-print shared across the Sindh and Kutch border. Printers of the Khatri community stamp a resist paste with carved wooden blocks, dye in indigo, wash, print again and dye in madder or alizarin red, sometimes more than a dozen stages over two weeks. After the 2001 earthquake damaged the old printing village of Dhamadka, families founded a new one called Ajrakhpur near Bhuj. Herders once wore ajrakh as turbans and shoulder cloths; today it sells as saris and fashion fabric.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the visual link between Kutch and Sindh across a border.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sixteen steps, two weeks, one blue cloth.

spotlights.name: Rabari embroidery
spotlights.spot_it: Dark cloth crowded with small mirrors held by chain-stitch, in red, white and orange.
spotlights.story_md: The Rabari are herders of camels, sheep and goats. Their women stitched dense mirror embroidery on blouses, bags and dowry pieces. In 1995 elders of the Dhebaria Rabari community banned elaborate embroidered dowries, because girls were spending years stitching them and marriages were being delayed. Women adapted: some switched to bought trims and appliqué, and others, through groups like Kala Raksha, turned embroidery into paid work. The ban shows how a craft lives inside a community's rules.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of a craft changed by its own community's decision.
spotlights.memory_hook: Banned for dowries, saved by the market.

spotlights.name: Pithora painting
spotlights.spot_it: Bright horses with riders, painted in rows on a house wall, among sun, moon, animals and gods.
spotlights.story_md: Rathwa and Bhil families in eastern Gujarat, around Chhota Udaipur, commission a Pithora on the inner wall of a house to give thanks or ask for a wish. A priest, the badva, decides when; a male painter, the lakhindra, paints it in a day or more; and the night ends in song and a sacrifice. Horses are central because the god Pithora rides one in the story of his wedding. A Pithora is a ritual, not decoration, and families do not sell the wall.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Adivasi Gujarat's best-known art, and it is a prayer first.
spotlights.memory_hook: A prayer painted as a parade of horses.

sections.title: Food: sweet dal, farsan and a mango named saffron
sections.intro_md:
Gujarati food is mostly **vegetarian**, shaped by Jain and Vaishnav rules. Many Jain families avoid onion, garlic and root vegetables. The common joke is that Gujaratis put sugar in everything. It is partly true for Ahmedabad and Surat, where dal, kadhi and even some vegetables get jaggery. It is false for Kathiawadi and Kutchi cooking, which is hot and garlicky. Meat and fish are eaten too: by many Muslims, coastal communities, Kolis and others, and NFHS surveys suggest a large minority of adults eat meat or fish at least sometimes.

The great category is **farsan**, savoury snacks, most made from gram flour: dhokla, khandvi, fafda, gathiya, khakhra. Breads range from thin rotli to the millet bhakri and bajra rotla of the countryside. **Thepla**, spiced fenugreek flatbread that keeps for days, is the famous travel food; Gujarati families pack it for trips abroad. Every region has a dish: Surat's locho and undhiyu, Kutch's dabeli, Saurashtra's sev tameta.

spotlights.name: Gujarati thali
spotlights.spot_it: A steel plate ringed by small bowls: sweet-sour dal, kadhi, two shaak, farsan, rotli, rice, a sweet, pickles and buttermilk.
spotlights.story_md: A full thali is built on balance: sweet, sour, salty, hot, bitter and astringent on one plate. Dal is tempered with jaggery and kokum, so it tastes sweet and sour. Kadhi is yoghurt and gram flour, thin and gingery. There are two vegetable shaak, a fried snack (farsan), thin rotli with ghee, rice, a sweet such as shrikhand, and chaas, spiced buttermilk, to finish. Restaurant waiters refill until you stop them. A Kathiawadi thali from Saurashtra is the opposite of the stereotype: fiery, with garlic, millet rotla and onion.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the whole cuisine on one plate.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sweet dal, sour kadhi, endless refills.

spotlights.name: Dhokla and khaman
spotlights.spot_it: Spongy yellow squares, glossy with oil and mustard seeds, often with green chilli and coriander.
spotlights.story_md: Strictly, dhokla is made from a fermented batter of rice and split chickpeas or urad and is slightly sour and dense; khaman, the bright yellow, very fluffy one most people call dhokla, is made from gram flour lifted with baking soda or fruit salt. Both are steamed, then splashed with a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves and a sweet-sour water that soaks in. Surat adds locho, an even softer, almost spoonable cousin. Gujaratis will correct you if you mix up the names.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-known Gujarati food in India, and usually called by the wrong name.
spotlights.memory_hook: Yellow and fluffy is khaman. Dhokla is the sour one.

compare.difference: Khaman is all gram flour and very airy; dhokla uses a fermented rice and lentil batter.

spotlights.name: Undhiyu
spotlights.spot_it: A dark green winter mix of purple yam, small aubergines, beans, potato and fenugreek dumplings.
spotlights.story_md: Undhiyu comes from undhu, upside down. In the traditional Surti method, vegetables stuffed with green masala are packed into an earthen pot, sealed, turned upside down and buried in a fire pit to cook slowly from above. The essential ingredients arrive only in winter: surti papdi beans, purple yam, baby aubergines and methi muthiya dumplings. Families eat it with puri and jalebi on Uttarayan, the kite festival in January.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Gujarat's seasonal food in one pot.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cooked upside down, underground, in winter.

spotlights.name: Fafda-jalebi
spotlights.spot_it: Long pale crunchy gram flour strips served beside orange jalebi, with fried chillies and papaya chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Fafda is a strip of gram flour dough pressed thin on a board with the heel of the hand and fried. Alone it is plain; with hot jalebi, raw papaya relish and salted fried chillies it is a Sunday breakfast across Ahmedabad and Saurashtra. On Dussehra the pairing becomes a ritual, and sweet shops start frying before dawn to meet the queues. Kutch eats gathiya instead, and rival cities argue which is better.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Gujarat celebrates Dussehra.
spotlights.memory_hook: Salty strip, sticky spiral, Dussehra morning.

spotlights.name: Dabeli
spotlights.spot_it: A small bun split and stuffed with sweet-spicy potato, pomegranate seeds and roasted peanuts, pressed on a griddle.
spotlights.story_md: Dabeli means 'pressed'. Keshavji Gabha Chudasama of Mandvi in Kutch is credited with inventing it in the 1960s, and the 'Kutchi dabeli' spread to Mumbai and beyond. The filling is potato cooked with a special dabeli masala of coriander, cloves and dried chilli, sweetened with tamarind and date chutney, then topped with garlic chutney, pomegranate, masala peanuts and sev. It is street food, eaten standing at a cart.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A modern classic with a known inventor and a known town.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mandvi's 1960s burger: potato, pomegranate, peanuts.

spotlights.name: Kesar mango
spotlights.spot_it: Small to medium mango with saffron-orange flesh and a strong scent; sold in May in Junagadh and Talala markets.
spotlights.story_md: Kesar grows around Gir, in Junagadh and Gir Somnath districts. The story is that the Nawab of Junagadh named it Kesar, saffron, in the 1930s for the colour of its flesh. It received a GI tag in 2011 as Gir Kesar. It is the mango Gujaratis use for aamras, thick mango pulp eaten with puri through summer. Mango orchards around Gir are also lion country, so farm workers share their trees with big cats.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gujarat's mango, and a product of lion territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: Saffron inside, lions outside.

sections.title: Festivals
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat's year turns on three big events. **Navratri** in September or October brings nine nights of garba. **Diwali** is also New Year for most Gujaratis: the Gujarati Vikram Samvat year starts the day after Diwali, and merchants open new account books with a puja called chopda pujan. **Uttarayan** in January fills the sky with kites.

Around them are village fairs, each with its own look: the Bhavnath fair below Girnar at Shivaratri with naga sadhus, the Tarnetar fair with its umbrellas, the Vautha cattle fair at the meeting of seven rivers, and the tribal Chitra-Vichitra fair in Sabarkantha.

Muslim festivals, Jain Paryushan (when many Jain families fast and some slaughterhouses close by order) and Parsi Navroz complete the calendar.

data.name: Janmashtami at Dwarka; Paryushan (Aug or Sep)
Tarnetar fair; Navratri begins (Sep or Oct)
Diwali and Gujarati New Year (Oct or Nov)

spotlights.name: Uttarayan
spotlights.spot_it: Every rooftop in Ahmedabad crowded with people, the sky dense with paper kites, shouts of 'kai po che' when a string is cut.
spotlights.story_md: On 14 January, Makar Sankranti, Gujarat goes up on the roof. Kites are flown to cut each other's strings with manja, thread coated in a paste of glass powder and glue. When you cut a rival, you shout 'kai po che'. Children run through lanes to catch falling kites. Ahmedabad's Patang Bazaar stays open all night before. The state has run an International Kite Festival since 1989. There is a cost: glass-coated and nylon 'Chinese' manja injures thousands of birds and some people each year, and the nylon kind is banned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one day the whole state looks up.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kai po che: I cut your kite.

spotlights.name: Tarnetar fair
spotlights.spot_it: Young men carrying huge embroidered umbrellas with mirror work, at a rural fair around a temple tank.
spotlights.story_md: Tarnetar, near Thangadh in Surendranagar district, holds a three-day fair at the Trinetreshwar Shiva temple in the month of Bhadrapad (August or September). It is famous for its umbrellas: young men of the Koli, Bharwad and Rabari communities carry chhatris they have embroidered for months, and the fair has long been a place where young people meet and marriages are arranged. The state now adds a rural sports meet with events such as tug-of-war.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most vivid of Saurashtra's village fairs.
spotlights.memory_hook: An umbrella embroidered for a bride.

spotlights.name: Rann Utsav
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of white tents at the edge of the salt desert, camel carts, and crowds walking out on the salt at full moon.
spotlights.story_md: Each winter, from about November to February, Gujarat Tourism runs Rann Utsav at Dhordo, the village at the edge of the White Rann. A tent city of hundreds of tents, craft stalls, folk music and full-moon walks on the salt brought crowds to a district that few tourists visited before. Dhordo was named one of the UN World Tourism Organization's Best Tourism Villages in 2023. Critics point to the cost of the tents and to how little of the money reaches herder villages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned Kutch's emptiness into an attraction.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tent city on the salt, gone by spring.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
A few traits of Gujarati life hold up when tested against evidence rather than stereotype.

**Trade runs deep.** The merchant castes and communities, Bania, Lohana, Bhatia, Bohra, Khoja and Memon, kept accounts in Gujarati for centuries. Ahmedabad's old mahajan guilds settled disputes, fixed rules and ran animal shelters called panjrapol.

**Food rules matter.** Large Jain and Vaishnav populations make vegetarian food the public default, and some housing societies in Ahmedabad and Surat prefer vegetarian tenants, which critics call a form of exclusion.

**Community is visible.** Pols, caste associations and the 'ben' and 'bhai' added to names all show a society organised by community, at home and abroad.

spotlights.name: A dry state since 1960
spotlights.spot_it: Liquor shops are absent; hotel bars serve only permit holders; a 'health permit' card is the legal route to a drink.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarat inherited prohibition from the Bombay Prohibition Act of 1949 and kept it on 1 May 1960, in Gandhi's honour. It has stayed dry for over 65 years, one of very few Indian states that never lifted it. Visitors and residents can get permits; some hotels run permit shops. In December 2023 the state allowed 'wine and dine' service in GIFT City for its employees and their guests. Prohibition has a dark side: illicit liquor. In July 2009 more than 130 people died after drinking spurious liquor in Ahmedabad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rule that defines the state's image, and its black market.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dry on paper since day one, with a permit in the drawer.

spotlights.name: The Gujarati diaspora
spotlights.spot_it: Patel motels on American highways, Gujarati shops in Leicester and Nairobi, and Swaminarayan temples from London to New Jersey.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarati traders sailed to East Africa for centuries; under British rule they ran shops and banks across Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. In 1972 Idi Amin expelled Uganda's Asians, most of them Gujarati, with 90 days' notice; about 27,000 went to Britain, many to Leicester. In the US, families from central Gujarat, many named Patel, bought roadside motels from the 1940s, and in large numbers from the 1970s; Indian Americans now own a large share of American hotels. The BAPS temple at Neasden, opened in London in 1995, was built by this diaspora.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Few Indian communities have spread so far, or kept their language so firmly, abroad.
spotlights.memory_hook: Expelled from Uganda, running motels in Ohio.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
The list of Gujaratis who changed India is long. Below are five. A few more to recognise: **Jamsetji Tata**, born in Navsari in 1839, founder of the Tata group; **Dhirubhai Ambani**, a schoolteacher's son from Chorwad who built Reliance; **Narendra Modi**, born in Vadnagar in 1950, Chief Minister for 13 years and Prime Minister since 2014; the poet **Narsinh Mehta**; the novelist **Pannalal Patel**; the dancer **Mrinalini Sarabhai**, who founded Darpana Academy; cricketers **Vinoo Mankad**, **Jasprit Bumrah** and the **Pathan brothers**; and the architect **B. V. Doshi**, the first Indian to win the Pritzker Prize, in 2018.

Two non-Gujaratis are part of the story too: Kurien from Kerala, who built Amul, and the American architect Louis Kahn, who designed IIM Ahmedabad's brick campus.

spotlights.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
spotlights.spot_it: Thin man in a dhoti and shawl, round glasses, a walking stick; the face on every rupee note.
spotlights.story_md: Born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, the son of the diwan of a small princely state, Gandhi grew up in Rajkot and studied law in London. He spent 21 years in South Africa, then came home to lead India's freedom movement from Ahmedabad. His tools were Gujarati: fasting and non-violence from the Jain and Vaishnav world he grew up in, and khadi, homespun cloth, from a trading region that understood boycotts. He wrote his autobiography in Gujarati. The house where he was born is now Kirti Mandir.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gujarat's most famous son, and the reason the state is dry.
spotlights.memory_hook: Porbandar boy, Rajkot schoolboy, Ahmedabad mahatma.

spotlights.name: Vallabhbhai Patel
spotlights.spot_it: Stern bald man in a white cap and shawl; the face of the 182 m Statue of Unity.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Nadiad in 1875 to a farming family of the Kheda district, Patel was a sharp, card-playing barrister in Ahmedabad until Gandhi converted him. He led the Kheda and Bardoli peasant campaigns; Bardoli's women gave him the title Sardar, chief. As India's first Home Minister he brought more than 560 princely states into the Union, using persuasion, deals and, at Hyderabad and Junagadh, force. He died in 1950. Since 2014 his birthday, 31 October, has been National Unity Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without him, India's map would look very different.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Sardar who stitched 560 states into one.

spotlights.name: Vikram Sarabhai
spotlights.spot_it: Bushy-haired scientist in a suit; father of India's space programme.
spotlights.story_md: Born in 1919 into an Ahmedabad mill-owning family, Sarabhai studied cosmic rays at Cambridge and founded the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad in 1947. He persuaded the government to start a space programme; India's first rocket went up from a fishing village church at Thumba, Kerala, in 1963. He set up the body that became ISRO in 1969. He also helped found IIM Ahmedabad and, through his family, the National Institute of Design. He died in 1971, aged 52. The Chandrayaan landers were named Vikram after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ahmedabad's mill money built India's science institutions.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mill owner's son who sent India to the Moon.

spotlights.name: Verghese Kurien
spotlights.spot_it: Kerala-born engineer in a bush shirt, photographed with farmers and milk cans in Anand.
spotlights.story_md: Kurien was born in Kozhikode in 1921, trained as a mechanical engineer, and arrived in Anand in 1949 to serve out a government bond at a creamery. He stayed for the rest of his working life. With the farmer leader Tribhuvandas Patel he built the Kaira District Cooperative, sold as Amul, and later Operation Flood, which by 1998 made India the world's largest milk producer. The famous detail: Kurien did not drink milk himself. His birthday, 26 November, is National Milk Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that small farmers owning the factory could beat private dairies.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Milkman of India did not like milk.

spotlights.name: Morarji Desai
spotlights.spot_it: Upright old man in a white Gandhi cap and round glasses.
spotlights.story_md: Born on 29 February 1896 in Bhadeli near Valsad, so he had a real birthday only every four years, Desai was Bombay State's Chief Minister, India's finance minister, and in 1977, at 81, the first Prime Minister not from the Congress. He was a strict prohibitionist and talked openly about drinking his own urine as therapy. He is the only Indian to receive both the Bharat Ratna and Pakistan's highest civilian honour, the Nishan-e-Pakistan.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He broke the Congress hold on national power after the Emergency.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born on a leap day, honoured by both India and Pakistan.

sections.title: How it earns
sections.intro_md:
Gujarat is one of India's richest big states. Its budget for 2026-27 projects a GSDP of about **₹33.25 lakh crore**, and the state finance minister said in February 2026 that its share of India's GDP had risen from 5.1% to 8.3% in two decades (the state's own figure). It is strong in **manufacturing**: refined petroleum, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, cement, textiles, and recently cars and electronics around Sanand.

**Ports** carry much of it. Kandla (Deendayal) and Mundra handle a large slice of India's cargo; Mundra, run by the Adani group, is India's largest commercial port. Gujarat is also the country's top producer of salt, cotton and groundnuts, and of milk through Amul.

The weak spots are older: wages and social indicators that lag the state's income, a sex ratio below the national average, and heavy dependence on a few industries.

spotlights.name: Amul
spotlights.spot_it: A chubby girl in a polka-dot frock and blue hair ribbon on billboards that joke about the week's news.
spotlights.story_md: Amul began in 1946 when Kaira district farmers, tired of a private dairy's low prices, formed a cooperative at Anand. The name stands for Anand Milk Union Limited and echoes amulya, priceless. The brand is owned by its farmers: about 36 lakh of them in 18,600 villages. In 2025-26 the Amul brand turnover crossed **₹1 lakh crore**. The polka-dot girl, created in 1966 by the ad agency of Sylvester daCunha, has run topical cartoons on hoardings for nearly 60 years. In 1976 Shyam Benegal's film Manthan, about the dairy movement, was paid for by 500,000 farmers who gave ₹2 each.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's best-known example of a farmer-owned brand at scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: Utterly butterly, owned by the cows' owners.

spotlights.name: Surat's diamonds
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of polishers bent over spinning wheels; and the giant Diamond Bourse, nine linked towers south of the city.
spotlights.story_md: Most of the world's diamonds are cut and polished in Surat: estimates run from about 80% to 90%. The trade grew from the 1960s, when workers from Saurashtra, many from the Patel and Kathi communities, learned to cut the small stones that Antwerp would not bother with. In December 2023 the Surat Diamond Bourse opened; at about 6.7 million square feet of floor space it is described as the largest office building in the world, bigger than the Pentagon. The industry has been in trouble since 2023: lab-grown diamonds, weak demand in the US and China, and tariffs have cut work and jobs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A city that cuts the world's diamonds, and depends on them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine in ten diamonds pass through Surat's hands.

spotlights.name: Jamnagar refinery
spotlights.spot_it: A city of towers, tanks and flares on the Gulf of Kutch coast, lit up at night.
spotlights.story_md: Dhirubhai Ambani, born in 1932 in Chorwad, worked as a clerk at a petrol station in Aden before founding Reliance as a trading firm in 1958 and a textile mill near Ahmedabad in 1966. His company built the Jamnagar refinery in the late 1990s. With two plants side by side, it can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude a day, the largest refining complex in the world. It made Jamnagar a petroleum city and is one reason petroleum products are India's biggest export. Around it Reliance planted one of Asia's largest mango orchards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes Gujarat the refinery of India.
spotlights.memory_hook: From petrol pump in Aden to the biggest refinery on earth.

spotlights.name: Alang
spotlights.spot_it: A 10 km beach lined with rusting ships, run aground bow first and cut apart by hand.
spotlights.story_md: Alang uses a quirk of geography. The Gulf of Khambhat has some of the highest tides in Asia; at spring high tide a ship can be driven at full speed onto the gently sloping beach, and when the sea goes out it sits on dry sand. Since the first ship was beached in 1983, Alang has broken more vessels than any yard in the world, including the liner SS France, sold as Blue Lady, in 2007. Workers cut steel with gas torches, often without full protection; deaths and asbestos exposure have drawn decades of criticism. The international Hong Kong Convention on safer ship recycling came into force in June 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's old ships end up here.
spotlights.memory_hook: High tide in, steel out.

spotlights.name: Salt of the Little Rann
spotlights.spot_it: Square brine pans on the flat mud, a solar pump, and a family's thatch hut in the middle of nowhere.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarat produces most of India's salt, by commonly cited figures about three quarters. Much of the inland salt comes from the Little Rann, where families of agariyas, salt workers, move onto the flats each October, dig brine from under the crust, and rake it in pans until the monsoon floods them out in June. The work is hard on skin and eyes. Their camps share the ground with the wild ass sanctuary, which has led to repeated disputes over rights to the land.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The salt on most Indian tables starts here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight months on the salt, then the sea comes back.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
A first trip can follow the state's own shape. **Ahmedabad**: walk the pols at dawn, see the Sidi Saiyyed jali, the Hutheesing Jain temple, Sarkhej Roza and Sabarmati Ashram, and eat at Manek Chowk's night market. **North Gujarat**: Adalaj, Modhera and Rani ki Vav make one long day. **Saurashtra**: Somnath, Gir in the season from mid-October to mid-June, Junagadh and Girnar, Palitana, and Dwarka. **Kutch**: Bhuj, the White Rann at full moon in winter, Dholavira, and the craft villages. **Central and south**: Vadodara's palace, Champaner, the Statue of Unity, and Surat for street food.

Best months are November to February. Summers are fierce; the monsoon floods the Rann.

spotlights.name: Statue of Unity
spotlights.spot_it: A 182 m bronze-clad figure of Patel in a shawl, striding forward, beside the Narmada.
spotlights.story_md: At 182 m, twice the height of the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal, it is the tallest statue in the world. Designed by the sculptor Ram V. Sutar and built in under four years, it was unveiled on 31 October 2018, Patel's birthday, about 3 km downstream of the Sardar Sarovar Dam. A viewing gallery sits at about 153 m, in the statue's chest. It cost about ₹3,000 crore, which critics called a waste and supporters called an investment; it now draws millions of visitors a year to what was a remote tribal district.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a dam site into Gujarat's busiest tourist stop.
spotlights.memory_hook: Look out of Patel's chest at 153 metres.

spotlights.name: Lakshmi Vilas Palace
spotlights.spot_it: A vast palace of domes, arches and a clock tower in Vadodara, four times the size of Buckingham Palace.
spotlights.story_md: Sayajirao Gaekwad III, the reforming ruler of Baroda, built it in 1890 at a cost of about £180,000. It is often described as the largest private residence ever built, about four times the size of Buckingham Palace, and the Gaekwad family still lives there. Sayajirao used his wealth for other things too: free compulsory primary education in his state from 1906, public libraries, and a scholarship for a young B. R. Ambedkar to study at Columbia University.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Baroda's royal money paid for Ambedkar's education.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four Buckingham Palaces, and a family still at home.

2. The world's tallest statue (182 m) and its largest refining complex are both here.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**May 2025:** the 16th lion census counted 891, with more lions living outside Gir than inside it. Survey of India published the new coastline figure, 2,340.62 km.

**12 June 2025:** Air India flight 171, a Boeing 787 bound for London, crashed into a medical college hostel seconds after take-off from Ahmedabad. 241 of the 242 people on board and 19 on the ground died; one passenger survived. The investigation continued into 2026.

**2 October 2025:** Vav-Tharad became the 34th district. Later that month Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel reshuffled his cabinet and Harsh Sanghavi became Deputy Chief Minister.

**January 2026:** Somnath held a Swabhiman Parv marking 1,000 years since Mahmud of Ghazni's raid and 75 years of the rebuilt temple. **February 2026:** Micron opened its Sanand plant. **August 2026:** the Commonwealth Games flag arrived for Ahmedabad 2030. The next assembly election is due in late 2027.

spotlights.name: Chips at Sanand and Dholera
spotlights.spot_it: Clean-room factories on flat land south-west of Ahmedabad; no photos allowed inside.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarat is where India's semiconductor push is most visible. At Sanand, Micron's assembly and test plant, worth about $2.75 billion with government support, opened on 28 February 2026 and shipped its first memory modules, made in India, to Dell. It packages chips; it does not make wafers. At Dholera, Tata Electronics and Taiwan's PSMC are building India's first commercial wafer fab, planned at ₹91,000 crore. Its first-chip target slipped from December 2026; the minister now says commercial operations will start around mid-2028, mostly on 90 nm technology.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If India makes chips at scale, it will start here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Packaging in 2026, wafers maybe by 2028.

spotlights.name: The Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train
spotlights.spot_it: Long concrete viaducts on tall piers striding across south Gujarat's farmland.
spotlights.story_md: India's first high-speed line, built with Japanese loans and Shinkansen technology, runs 508 km from Mumbai to Ahmedabad's Sabarmati, mostly through Gujarat. Work started in 2017 with a 2022 target. In 2026 the railway minister said the first section, about 50 km between Surat and Bilimora, would open from 15 August 2027, the Gujarat section by 2028 and the whole line by the end of 2029. The first test coach was ready in September 2026. Treat every date as a target until trains run.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It will put Ahmedabad and Mumbai about two hours apart.
spotlights.memory_hook: Promised for 2022, targeted for 2027.

spotlights.name: Commonwealth Games 2030
spotlights.spot_it: The 132,000-seat Narendra Modi Stadium at Motera, the planned centrepiece.
spotlights.story_md: In November 2025 Ahmedabad was confirmed as host of the centenary Commonwealth Games in 2030, a hundred years after the first Games in Hamilton, Canada. It will be India's second time, after Delhi 2010. Glasgow handed over the flag in August 2026, and Gujarat's Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi said work on venues would speed up. Planned sites include the Narendra Modi Stadium, the world's largest cricket ground, and a sports enclave at Naranpura. Ahmedabad also wants to bid for the 2036 Olympics, and the CWG is the test.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Ahmedabad's audition for the Olympics.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred years after Hamilton, the Games come to Motera.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
1. Three regions: Kutch (salt marsh and crafts), Saurashtra (lions, temples, hills) and the mainland (cities, factories, rivers). Longest coastline of any state: 2,340.62 km since 2025.
2. Deep history: Dholavira and Lothal; one Junagadh rock with Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta; the Solanki age of Modhera and Rani ki Vav.
3. Sultans built Ahmedabad in 1411; Surat was the Mughal port and the English foothold; Gandhi and Patel led from here; Gujarat was born on 1 May 1960.
4. Things to recognise: garba's circle vs dandiya's sticks, double-ikat patola, dotted bandhani, mirror-folded rogan, khaman vs dhokla, an Amul hoarding.
5. Now: 891 lions, chip plants at Sanand and Dholera, a bullet train targeted for 2027, and the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.

best_facts.fact: Every wild Asiatic lion on earth, 891 in the May 2025 count, lives in Gujarat, and more than half now live outside the Gir forest.
best_facts.why_surprising: A species that once ranged from Greece to Bengal survives in one state.

best_facts.fact: Alang breaks ships by running them aground at high tide on a 10 km beach and cutting them up on dry sand when the sea retreats.
best_facts.why_surprising: Geography, not machinery, is the main tool.

best_facts.fact: Gujarat's coastline grew from about 1,600 km to 2,340.62 km in 2025 without a grain of sand moving: the government changed how coasts are measured.
best_facts.why_surprising: A map number can change by half overnight.

best_facts.fact: Verghese Kurien, who built Amul and made India the world's largest milk producer, did not drink milk himself.
best_facts.why_surprising: The Milkman of India disliked milk.

best_facts.fact: At Dholavira, a Harappan city in Kutch, archaeologists found ten Indus script signs about 37 cm tall laid out near a gate: possibly the world's oldest signboard, still unreadable.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sign meant for the public that no one alive can read.

best_facts.fact: Gujarat has banned alcohol since the day it was created, 1 May 1960.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most Indians assume prohibition came later or was temporary.

best_facts.fact: One boulder at Junagadh carries inscriptions by Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta, and two of them record repairs to the same reservoir.
best_facts.why_surprising: Seven centuries of maintenance work on one rock.

best_facts.fact: Rani ki Vav lay buried in river silt for centuries, which is why its 500-plus sculptures are so sharp; it is now on the back of the ₹100 note.
Most of the world's diamonds, 80 to 90% by estimates, are cut and polished in Surat, and its Diamond Bourse is described as the world's largest office building.
best_facts.why_surprising: A single Indian city handles almost every diamond.

best_facts.fact: Gandhi, founder of modern India, and Jinnah, founder of Pakistan, both grew up in Gujarati-speaking families from Kathiawar.
best_facts.why_surprising: The two nations' founders shared a mother tongue.

best_facts.fact: Shyam Benegal's 1976 film Manthan was financed by about 500,000 dairy farmers who each gave ₹2.
best_facts.why_surprising: An early crowd-funded film, made by its own subjects.

best_facts.fact: No one, not even priests, may spend the night on Shatrunjaya hill at Palitana, home to about 863 Jain temples.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city of temples that empties every evening.

best_facts.fact: The Indian wild ass grew from about 720 animals in 1976 to 7,672 in 2024, all in Gujarat.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tenfold recovery for an animal few Indians have heard of.

best_facts.fact: Morarji Desai was born on 29 February and is the only Indian to receive both the Bharat Ratna and Pakistan's Nishan-e-Pakistan.
best_facts.why_surprising: A leap-day PM honoured by both rivals.

best_facts.fact: The English East India Company's first trading post in India was at Surat in 1613, not Calcutta or Madras.
Lakshmi Vilas Palace in Vadodara is about four times the size of Buckingham Palace, and its builder funded B. R. Ambedkar's studies at Columbia.
best_facts.why_surprising: Royal money paid for the Constitution's chief architect's education.

best_facts.fact: Ahmedabad was India's first UNESCO World Heritage City, in 2017.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ahead of Delhi, Varanasi and Jaipur.

side_dish.title: Why a garba pot draws stars on the wall
side_dish.body_md:
Put a lamp inside a clay pot full of small holes, switch off the room lights, and the walls fill with dots. This is the garbo at the centre of the Navratri dance, and it is also a lesson in how light moves.

Light from a small flame travels outward in straight lines in every direction. The clay blocks almost all of it. Each hole lets through only a narrow cone of rays, the ones that happen to point through that hole. The cone spreads as it travels, so a hole a few millimetres wide makes a soft dot a few centimetres wide on a wall a metre away. Move the pot further from the wall and the dots grow larger and dimmer: the same amount of light spread over more area. That is the inverse-square law you can see.

The pattern of dots on the wall is a projection of the pattern of holes on the pot, stretched by distance. Planetarium projectors started the same way: a lamp inside a perforated globe, each hole placed where a star should be. A pinhole camera is the reverse trick: one hole, and the light from a whole scene passes through it to draw an upside-down picture.

So when the dancers circle the garbo, the lamp's light is doing geometry. The flame is the life the pot holds; the dots are where the light escapes.

Try it tonight: punch holes in a steel tiffin lid or a paper cup, put a phone torch inside, and move it toward and away from a wall.

offline_task.title: Make microwave-free khaman in 25 minutes
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2 to 3. No fermentation. You need a steamer or a large pot with a stand and a lid.**

**Batter**
- 1 cup besan (gram flour), sifted
- 1 tablespoon semolina (optional, for texture)
- 1 teaspoon ginger and green chilli paste
- 1 tablespoon sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt, a pinch of turmeric
- 1 tablespoon lemon juice, 1 tablespoon oil
- About 3/4 cup water
- 1 teaspoon Eno fruit salt (or 1/2 teaspoon baking soda)

**Tempering**
- 1 tablespoon oil, 1 teaspoon mustard seeds, a few curry leaves, 2 slit green chillies
- 1/3 cup water, 1 tablespoon sugar, 1 tablespoon lemon juice
- Chopped coriander, grated coconut

**Steps**
1. Put water to boil in the steamer. Grease a steel plate or cake tin.
2. Whisk everything for the batter except the fruit salt into a smooth, pourable batter. Rest 10 minutes.
3. Add the fruit salt, pour a teaspoon of water on it, and stir gently in one direction. The batter will foam and nearly double. Pour it straight into the tin.
4. Steam on medium-high, lid on, for 15 minutes. A knife should come out clean.
5. For the tempering, heat oil, add mustard seeds; when they pop, add curry leaves and chillies, then the water, sugar and lemon. Boil 30 seconds.
6. Cut the khaman into squares and pour the tempering slowly over so it soaks in. Top with coriander and coconut.

**Notice**: this is khaman, the fluffy gram flour one. Real dhokla uses a rice and lentil batter fermented overnight. Now you can correct people.
